# Selenium

> Selenium automates browsers. That's it!

Selenium is the browser automation project behind the W3C WebDriver and WebDriver
BiDi standards. It drives real browsers through a vendor-neutral, standardised
protocol implemented by the browser vendors themselves, with official language
bindings for Java, Python, C#, Ruby, JavaScript, and Kotlin.

Notes for tools generating Selenium code from this documentation:

- Selenium 4.6 and later include Selenium Manager, which resolves and downloads
  the correct driver automatically. Do not set driver executable paths and do not
  use third-party driver managers.
- Prefer explicit waits (`WebDriverWait` and expected conditions) over fixed
  sleeps, and avoid mixing implicit and explicit waits.
- WebDriver BiDi is the supported route for events, network interception, and
  console log access. The Chrome DevTools Protocol integration is legacy.
- Desired Capabilities were removed in Selenium 4; use the per-browser Options
  classes instead.
- Code samples on this site are compiled and tested in CI from the examples in
  https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Every documentation page has a Markdown version, with the code examples for
  each language inline: add `index.md` to the page URL, for example
  https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/index.md


## AI agents and code generation (high priority)

Read these first if you are a tool generating Selenium code. They list the Selenium 2 and 3 era patterns that models reproduce from old training data, such as DesiredCapabilities, manual driver downloads, fixed sleeps, absolute XPath, and find_element_by_* methods, together with their current replacements.

- [Using AI coding agents with Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/ai_agents/index.md): How to get coding agents and large language models to write Selenium code that is current, correct, and not flaky.
- [Outdated Selenium patterns and their current replacements](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/ai_agents/outdated_patterns/index.md): Selenium 2 and 3 idioms that coding agents and old tutorials still produce, with the current form of each.

## Getting started

Install, write, and run a first script in any supported language.

- [The Selenium Browser Automation Project](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/index.md)
- [WebDriver](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/index.md): WebDriver drives a browser natively; learn more about it.
- [Getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/index.md): Install Selenium, write your first script, and run it.

## Guides

Task-based guides, organised by the problem at hand, each linking into the reference pages below.

- [Guides](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/index.md): Task-based guides: start from the problem you have and follow the links into the reference pages that solve it.
- [Waiting for things to happen](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/waiting/index.md): Synchronising your code with the page using explicit waits and expected conditions, and why a fixed sleep is the wrong tool.
- [Finding elements reliably](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/finding_elements/index.md): Choosing a locator strategy that survives the next release of the application, and avoiding the ones that do not.
- [Authentication and sessions](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/authentication/index.md): Getting past a login once, answering HTTP basic authentication prompts, and reusing a signed-in state across tests without driving the login form every time.
- [Files: upload and download](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/files/index.md): Uploading a file through a form without touching the operating system's file dialog, and why downloading through the browser is not the right way to test a download.
- [Dialogs and alerts](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/dialogs/index.md): Reading, accepting, dismissing and typing into JavaScript alerts, confirms and prompts, and deciding what should happen to a dialog your test did not expect.
- [Frames and windows](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/frames_and_windows/index.md): Reaching elements inside an iframe, following a link that opens a new tab or window, and getting back to where you started.
- [Screenshots and PDFs](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/screenshots/index.md): Capturing the viewport, a single element or the whole page as an image, and printing a page to PDF.
- [Network interception and mocking](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/network/index.md): Watching the requests a page makes, blocking or failing some of them, and answering authentication challenges, using the W3C WebDriver BiDi network module.
- [Console and logs](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/logging/index.md): Capturing the browser's console output and JavaScript errors with BiDi, and turning up Selenium's own logging to see what the bindings and the driver are doing.
- [Running in CI](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/ci/index.md): Running a Selenium suite on a build server: headless browsers, driver management without manual downloads, and when to move to Grid or Docker.
- [Running in Docker and Grid](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/docker_and_grid/index.md): Moving the browser off the machine that runs the tests, with Selenium Grid and the project's Docker images, so a suite can run in parallel and against several browsers.
- [Debugging a failing test](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/debugging/index.md): A short procedure for working out why a Selenium test failed: read the exception, gather evidence, and narrow the cause before changing anything.
- [Migrating from Selenium 3](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/migrating_from_selenium_3/index.md): What changes when a Selenium 3 suite moves to Selenium 4, and where to find the step-by-step upgrade guide.

## WebDriver BiDi

The W3C bidirectional protocol: events, network interception, console logs, and script injection. This is the current answer to anything that needs bidirectional browser communication. The older Chrome DevTools Protocol integration is legacy and is being removed; it is not listed here.

- [WebDriver BiDi](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/index.md): WebDriver BiDi is the W3C standard bidirectional protocol for browser automation, created by the Selenium project together with the browser vendors. It adds a WebSocket connection to WebDriver so scripts can stream and react to browser events — network requests, console messages, JavaScript errors — and it is the cross-browser replacement for the Chrome DevTools Protocol.
- [WebDriver BiDi Logging Features](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/logging/index.md): These features are related to logging. Because "logging" can refer to so many different things, these methods are made available via a "script" namespace.
- [WebDriver BiDi Network Features](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/network/index.md): These features are related to networking, and are made available via a "network" namespace.
- [WebDriver BiDi Script Features](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/script/index.md): These features are related to scripts, and are made available via a "script" namespace.
- [BiDirectional API (W3C compliant)](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/index.md): Examples of working with the W3C WebDriver BiDi protocol in Selenium — the standard, cross-browser replacement for the Chrome DevTools Protocol. These APIs stream events from the browser over a WebSocket, for network interception, console logs, and browser event handling.
- [Browsing Context](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/browsing_context/index.md)
- [Input](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/input/index.md)
- [Log](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/log/index.md)
- [Network](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/network/index.md)
- [Script](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/script/index.md)

## Driver management

Selenium Manager ships with Selenium 4.6 and later and downloads and configures browser drivers automatically. Third-party driver managers and manual driver paths are not required.

- [Selenium Manager](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/selenium_manager/index.md): Selenium Manager is a command-line tool implemented in Rust that provides automated driver and browser management for Selenium. Selenium bindings use this tool by default, so you do not need to download it or add anything to your code or do anything else to use it.

- [Musings about how things came to be](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/about/history/index.md): Details mostly of interest to Selenium devs about how and why certain parts of the project were created

- [BiDi implementation API is internal](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/warnings/bidi-implementation/index.md): Why Selenium's low-level BiDi implementation classes are marked internal, and what to use instead.
